slides.title: Variations of the Length Integral
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter as a single question about geodesics under pressure. A geodesic is already locally straight, but the lecture asks what nearby curves reveal about curvature, focal behavior, minimization, and the global shape of the manifold.

slides.title: Route Through The Chapter
slides.notes: Use this roadmap to keep the many named results from feeling disconnected. The course moves from an ordinary differential equation along one geodesic to global statements about covering maps and group actions. The connective tissue is always the same: vary a geodesic and read the resulting quadratic form.

slides.title: Variation Fields Are Linear Data
slides.notes: Start with the operational meaning of a variation field. Students should see that the chapter is not varying abstract formulas; it is differentiating an actual family of curves. The field X records the velocity with which each point on the original curve moves as the family parameter changes.

slides.title: The Jacobi Equation
slides.notes: Present the Jacobi equation as the linearization of geodesic motion, not as a mysterious second order equation. The same initial value logic as ordinary differential equations remains, but the coefficient term is curvature along the geodesic, so the equation is already geometric.

slides.title: Conjugate Points And The Exponential Map
slides.notes: Emphasize the two interchangeable diagnostics. Along the geodesic, conjugacy is detected by a Jacobi field with two zeros. In the tangent space, it is detected by the differential of the exponential map losing rank, which explains why conjugate points are where geodesic coordinates begin to fold.

slides.title: Riemannian Jacobi Fields Split Cleanly
slides.notes: Separate the tangential bookkeeping from the normal geometry. The tangential part largely reflects reparametrization, while the normal part records how nearby geodesics actually spread or refocus. This split also prepares students for the index form, where normal variations are the essential variations for endpoint problems.

slides.title: Index Integral Before Morse Theory
slides.notes: Introduce the index integral before naming the full Morse theorem. It is the second variation written as a symmetric bilinear form. The sign competition matters: derivative energy makes variations expensive, while positive curvature can make transverse variations reduce length and eventually signal conjugate points.

slides.title: Curvature Bounds Control Focusing
slides.notes: Explain comparison as a disciplined replacement for drawing intuition. Higher positive curvature bends geodesic families inward faster, while nonpositive curvature prevents the collapse needed for conjugate points. The chapter uses the index integral to prove these statements and then reuses them in global geometry.

slides.title: First Variation: Geodesics Are Critical
slides.notes: Pause on the distinction between critical and minimizing. First variation explains why geodesics are the only candidates for local shortest paths under fixed endpoints. It does not decide whether the candidate is stable, because a saddle point also has zero first derivative.

slides.title: Second Variation And Boundary Terms
slides.notes: The second variation slide should feel like a Hessian calculation with geometric coefficients. For fixed endpoints, boundary terms disappear and the index form becomes the central object. When endpoints move or the field is only piecewise smooth, the same formula explains the correction terms.

slides.title: Jacobi Fields Are Equality Cases
slides.notes: Make the equality statement memorable. Jacobi fields are not only solutions of a differential equation; they are precisely the directions where the second variation fails to see positive curvature of the length functional. This is the bridge from local ODE analysis to Morse index counting.

slides.title: Conjugacy Destroys Minimizing Beyond It
slides.notes: Connect the technical conjugate-point machinery to a concrete geometric consequence. A geodesic can remain critical past a conjugate point, but it can no longer be globally shortest on the longer segment. This is how curvature lower bounds become diameter bounds and compactness theorems.

slides.title: Morse Index Counts Conjugate Points
slides.notes: Treat the Morse index theorem as the accounting system for the chapter. The index form starts positive near the initial point. Each conjugate point is a crossing where new negative directions appear, and multiplicity records how many independent Jacobi fields vanish there.

slides.title: Cut Locus: Where Minimizers Stop
slides.notes: The cut locus packages minimization failure into a geometric object. At a cut point, either the geodesic has reached its first conjugate obstruction or a second minimizing geodesic has arrived. This gives a useful frontier between normal coordinates and the global topology of the manifold.

slides.title: The Exponential Cell And Examples
slides.notes: Use the tangent-space picture to make the cut function concrete. Before the boundary, the exponential map gives honest normal coordinates. On the boundary, either rank failure or competing minimizers appear. The examples show that the cut locus is sensitive to topology, not only to curvature.

slides.title: Nonpositive Curvature Removes Conjugacy
slides.notes: Now let the earlier machinery pay off globally. In nonpositive curvature, Jacobi fields do not refocus, so the exponential map has no conjugate-point singularities. Comparison then supplies distance control, and completeness upgrades the local statement into a covering result.

slides.title: Center Of Gravity And Fixed Points
slides.notes: The center-of-gravity construction is a pleasant surprise after the index theorem. Nonpositive curvature gives enough convexity to average points without linear structure. For a compact isometry group, average one orbit and use uniqueness to show the barycenter cannot move.

slides.title: Closing Checklist
slides.notes: End with a reusable protocol. For every theorem in this chapter, ask what is being varied, which endpoint conditions are imposed, what the Jacobi equation says, and how the sign of the index form changes. That habit turns the chapter from a list of results into one coherent variational machine.
